newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS-OPEC eyes quota freeze, Iraq oil sales.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-OPEC eyes quota freeze, Iraq oil sales.

text.p: A consensus was emerging at OPEC talks that began on Wednesday to freeze current output quotas probably for six months to extend a rally in world oil prices.

Ministers said the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries needed to exercise caution in setting 1997 production levels, amid doubts on how winter weather may affect petroleum demand and on the timing and volume of resumed Iraqi exports.
Iraq's chief delegate, Osama al-Hiti, told reporters he now expected that Baghdad would resume oil sales under a relaxed U.N. Gulf War embargo in "a matter of weeks".
Delegates say OPEC linchpin Saudia Arabia favours a quota freeze, despite violations by some of the 11 members, at least to the end of June.

Ministers who told reporters they favour a "rollover" included Iran's Gholamreza Aqazadeh. He said he would support a 12-month freeze, although Algeria's Amar Makhloufi said he thought that the consensus was for six months.
A brief plenary session of the 101st OPEC ministerial adjourned to 0900 GMT on Thursday when substantive discussion of quotas will begin. Ministers say the talks may end on Thursday.

Iran's Aqazadeh meanwhile aired the vexed matter of quota violating at bilateral talks with Erwin Arrieta of Venezuela, alleged to be most in excess, but said later that Arrieta "did not accept even one barrel of over-production".
Traders say OPEC would be best advised to sidestep thorny issues and avoid public haggling that might alarm a skittish futures market and jeopardise a surprise 1996 rally in prices.

Benchmark Brent Blend crude is trading now around $23 a barrel compared with only $18 back in June when OPEC last met, mainly because of a rush to fill depleted Western stocks of heating fuel ahead of what may be a harsh northern winter.

"OPEC is meeting against a backdrop that can only bring a smile to their lips", said Peter Gignoux, head of the London energy desk at brokers Smith Barney. "Oil is up five dollars. That is in itself an incentive to preserve the status quo".
Prices are strong in spite of both a revived prospect that the 1990 Gulf War ban on Iraqi exports may soon be relaxed and OPEC's own quota violations.

Alleged excess is said by Western monitors to have already propelled OPEC volume a million barrels daily above a ceiling agreed at 25.03 million, even before 800,000 extra that has been pencilled in for founder member Iraq begins to flow.
But delegates say Saudi Arabia feels the market can absorb more oil, because stocks are low and as a result of the delay so far on resumed Iraqi sales.
Iraq this week agreed to U.N. conditions that had held up implementing an oil-for-food accord to let it sell $2 billion worth of oil to help buy food and medicine.

Iraq's al-Hiti said in Vienna that only a pricing formula and "very minor technicalities" had now to be ironed out. He expected to export 700,000 to 800,000 barrels daily using up in full his OPEC quota allocation.
The weather is another imponderable.
Depending on its severity, the northern winter can swing petroleum demand by a million barrels daily, Barclays Bank economists note in their latest Commodities Survey.
They have raised their forecast for average 1996 prices to $20 per barrel from only $16.8 in 1995. But they add that "our view remains that prices are likely to ease next year".
Their view that they'll ease by maybe $1.0 is based on the "strong possibility" of revived Iraqi exports and a prospect of more supply from the North Sea, Asia and Latin America.
Outgoing OPEC president Rakan bin Salem bin Rakad opened the talks with a warning against complacency over prices.
He said in a speech that "we must guard against taking the situation for granted. As we are well aware market fortunes can change radically and rapidly..."
